How did you learn to ride a bike? You may have watched a sibling or friend on
their bikes. You may have gotten advice from Mom and Dad. But family and friends
can't really explain the remarkable mental and physical gymnastics of riding a
bike. No book or video can truly describe it.

Of course, you know you learnt to bike ride by trying to bike ride. It's a
process of making mistakes, falling off a lot, correcting mistakes, and falling
off much less. It's accomplished by lots of practice. By repeating and refining
your moves you gradually rewire your brain to perform the task of bike riding.
And sooner or later you're riding a bike without conscious thought.

This type of learning is called experiential learning, i.e., learning by
experiencing. What you learnt by watching your friend when bike riding or
listening to advice on bike riding is called observational learning, i.e.,
learning by observing, listening, reading, etc. Experiential learning is more
personal. You're more engaged and you're more invested.

Developing skills in physics problem solving is similar to learning to ride a
bike. It's best developed by trying to solve problems. Of course, some advice on
problem solving, like advice on bike riding, is also helpful. So here I'll try
to describe my process and steps in solving a problem.

To make the description of problem solving more concrete let's consider a
specific example of a problem from our textbook. As I read the problem I try to
build an image in my mind of the situation.

"A magician astonishes his applauding audience with two gravity-defying balls
that hang from strings at non-vertical angles (the audience is unaware the two
balls are electrically charged).

*[Original illustration (Canvas login
required)](https://uk.instructure.com/courses/2052198/files/104696697/preview)*

In the trick the two small, 0.04 g balls were suspended by two light, 34.0 cm
long strings from a common point. Given the balls had come to rest with each
string at an angle 7.3o to the vertical, find the magnitude of the charge on
each ball. Assume the balls have equal charge."

Firstly, my mental image is restricted to the things that are relevant to the
problem. The balls, strings and the geometry of their arrangement. Omitted are
the things that are superfluous to the problem. The magician, audience and the
applause and the trickery. I'm conscious of what quantities I'm told (masses,
lengths, angles) and what quantities I need to find (charges).

Importantly, my mental image is framed by a recognition of the context of the
problem. In this problem the balls are hanging at rest and therefore the sum of
the forces on each ball must be zero. The problem is therefore about the
equilibrium between the electrical, gravitational and tension forces that are
acting on each ball. This understanding is the heart of the solution to the
problem.

[Original illustration (Canvas login
required)](https://uk.instructure.com/courses/2052198/files/104696800/preview)

Finally, my mental image is abstracted. The small metallic balls became point
mass balls. The light strings become un-stretchable massless strings. The point
mass ball and un-stretchable massless string aren't real-life balls or real-life
strings. Rather they're invaluable approximations for physics reasoning.

Of course the challenge for me is explaining to you just how I knew what's
important and what's not, how I knew the problem is one of equilibrium of
forces, and how I knew to abstract the ball, string, etc. I believe this arises
from experience with solving many problems. By solving problems we teach
ourselves the concepts and priciples of physics and learn to recognize the
connections between problems. With practice this understanding becomes
habituated and unconscious. Like riding a bike.

If you're stuck with how to proceed ask yourself some questions. Is the problem
about calculating a force, an energy, a field, a potential, etc? Does the
problem give values of charges, currents, wavelength, frequencies, etc? What
you're told about and what you're asked about are the clues to the foundations
of the problem.

The next step in problem solving is sketching with pencil and paper your mental
image. Your sketch will incorporate both the relevant objects like balls,
strings, etc., and the relevant concepts like equilibrium, forces, etc. There's
something about making the sketch that helps to crystallize and clarify your
reasoning. It obliges the resolution of all the umm's and ahh's about what's
happening.

In sketching our problem I'd denote the mass m and charge q of the ball and I'd
denote the length L and angle theta of the string. I'd also sketch the three
forces - gravity, electricity and tension - that are act of the balls. I'd be
careful in sketching the directions of forces: the gravity attraction is
downwards towards the earth's center, the electrical repulsion is horizontal
between the two charged balls, and tension acts along each string's length.

After making the sketch I re-read the problem. One reason is double-checking my
initial interpretation of the physics problem. I sometimes discover I've
misunderstood something. I sometimes discover I've missed something.

Another reason to re-read the problem is to annotate your sketch with the given
values of the physical quantities. Sometimes we're directly told the mass of the
small metallic ball is 0.04 g or the length of the light string is 34.0 cm.
Sometimes these values are coded in statements like "a body at rest", "on a
smooth surface", etc. Sometimes you'll want to note a constant of nature that's
relevant, e.g., the acceleration of gravity, g, the speed of light, c.

The acts of drawing and annotating are a foundations for your solution to the
problem. They require a definiteness and preciseness in your description of the
physics problem and the underlying principles. It's akin to describing the
problem in your own words. It's analogous to digging a hole and pouring the
concrete for the construction of a house. Both solutions and houses may collapse
without sturdy foundations.

Almost certainly your conceptualization of the problem may be written as an
equation. In our example, conceiving a problem as based on equilibrium implies
the sum of forces is zero, \[equation missing in original\] ( a very basic
equation). As another example, conceiving a problem as based on energy
conservation implies the initial and final energies are equal, \[equation
missing in original\] (a very basic equation). Such equations are the core of
our solution of the problem - a foot-in-the-door in solving the problem.

All the hundreds of physics problems in physics textbooks involving
translational equilibrium have the common core of \[equation missing in
original\]. And all the hundreds of physics problems in physics textbooks
involving energy conservation have the common core of \[equation missing in
original\]. It's in this sense we say that physics describes a vast array of
natural phenomena through a small number of basic ideas and corresponding
equations.

Think about your grandma. When I think of mine my thoughts will wander to
related things. The short walk to her house, the cookies she made, the rabbits
she kept, and so on. These are things that I associate with my
grandma.\[equation missing in original\]

[Original illustration (Canvas login
required)](https://uk.instructure.com/courses/2052198/files/104696847/preview)

The next stage in problem solving involves expanding the core equation with
problem specifics through association. My thoughts wander from equilibrium to
gravity, electricity, tension, and then to forces being vectors, and then to how
gravity works, and then to how electricity works, and so on. These are things
I'm associating with the grandma.

In expanding the equation \[equation missing in original\] I'd write down the
individual gravitational, electrical and tension forces that sum to zero. I'd
utilize my understanding of geometry, trigonometry and vectors to express the
equilibrium of forces in the horizontal direction and the vertical directions.
And I'd also expand each force using equations that represent my understanding
of how they work, i.e., \[equation missing in original\], \[equation missing in
original\]/r2.

By the tailoring of the core equation(s) to our particular problem we're
constructing the relationship between the quantities we're told (the knowns m,
L, \[equation missing in original\]) and the quantities we want (the unknown q).
At this stage the physics-focused problem has morphed into a algebra-centered
problem of solving equations for unknown variables, i.e., algebra.

Algebra is the manipulation of symbols rather than manipulation of numbers. (We
owe our thanks for the birth of the discipline to the Islamic Golden Age, the
"House of Wisdom", and famous book "Al-Jabr".) I think of algebra as like
balance weighing scales. If you add or subtract an equal weight from both sides
of the weigh scales it remains in balance. If you multiply or divide the weights
on both sides of the weighing scales it remains in balance. The same with
equations and adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing on both sides of the
equal sign. You've got to keep the equation balanced to successfully find the
unknown quantity.

In some cases a problem's solution involves one concept, one equation and rather
straightforward algebra of rearranging the equation to find the unknown. In
other cases a problem's solution involves multiple concepts, multiple equations
and more complicated algebra involving ordering, combining and rearranging the
equations to find the unknown(s).

In our example, I used the equation (1), describing equilibrium in the vertical
direction, to replace the tension in equation (2), describing equilibrium in the
horizontal direction, in terms of known quantities (m, g and \[equation missing
in original\]). This yields a 'blended' equation that can be rearranged to find
the unknown charge, q.

[Original illustration (Canvas login
required)](https://uk.instructure.com/courses/2052198/files/104696860/preview)

One piece of advice. It's almost always best to leave the substitution of
numbers into equations to the end of the problem. In working with equations it's
easier to follow the steps when physical quantities are represented by symbols
not numbers. We all make mistakes and its easier to find the mistake with
symbols than numbers as a symbol is a reminder to its meaning while a number is
a poker-face to its meaning. You'll save a lot of hair-pulling by working with
symbols.

Another piece of advice. My first attempt at solving a problem - from underlying
concepts and core equations to specific details and finding unknowns - sometimes
succeeds and sometimes fails. It's common to have to explore a number of dead
ends before finding the correct path to solving a problem. This is normal for
everyone. Whether it's doing your homework or running a marathon you'll need
some persistence.

Once you've obtained a solution it's important to check it. Does the magnitude
make sense? Does of the sign / direction make sense? If you're asked to
calculate the mass of a elephant and you obtain 2.5 grams you know you've made a
mistake somewhere. If you're asked to calculate the height of a skyscraper and
you obtain 2.5 centimeters you also know you've made a mistake somewhere. In our
example the a charge of 6.4 nano-Coulombs is typical of charging by rubbing.
Charges of Coulomb's, kilo-Coulombs, or mega-Coulombs would be ridiculously
large.

You can also check your equations are sensible. In our example we found that
\[equation missing in original\] . The equation 'tells us' that the larger the
mass of the balls the larger the charge of the balls. This makes sense as a
greater electrical force must accompany a greater gravitational force in order
to maintain the equilibrium of forces. You might also check the dimensions. On
the righthand side we've r \[L\], m \[M\], g \[L/T2\], k\[ML3/T2Q2\], \[equation
missing in original\]\[-\] where \[L\], \[T\], \[M\], \[Q\] are the fundamental
dimensions of space, time, mass and charge, respectively. That sounds like
dimensional-spaghetti but actually the righthand side dimension simplify to
\[Q\] the dimension of q.

Often there's different ways to solve a given problem. In our example, after
writing down the equations describing equilibrium in the horizontal / vertical
directions, I could have computed the gravitational force on the ball via FG =
mg, the tension force on the ball via T = FG / cos \[equation missing in
original\], and then the electric force on the ball FE = T sin\[equation missing
in original\] (the latter two equations follow from horizontal / vertical
equilibrium). Then I could solve for q using Coulomb's law FE = k q2/r2 as FE,
q, r are all known. This approach is like taking a series of small steps to the
answer rather than one big leap to the answer. It has the advantage of simpler
algebra in each step but the disadvantage that the relation between the unknown
charge q and the known variables m, L, \[equation missing in original\], etc.,
gets lost.

Finally, a general remark on problem solving. As human beings we build mental
models of the surrounding world. Our models incorporate our perceptions and
interpretations of things from how nature works to how people behave. We all
come to class with individualized models and some of our physics conceptions are
correct and some of our physics conceptions are incorrect.

A problem that's simple to solve isn't really a problem. We learn by struggling
and persevering to solve a problem. Struggling is when we confront and correct
our misconceptions and misunderstanding. That's why the experiential learning of
problem solving is so valuable - both in physics class and in everyday life.
